anchorCharts.name: Characters
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about characters.
anchorCharts.body: Characters are the people, animals, or beings in a story. To understand a character, look at what the character says, does, thinks, wants, and learns.
ex: If a character shares food during a storm, that action shows kindness.
If a character brags but later apologizes, the character changes from proud to humble.
If a character keeps trying after a mistake, that shows determination.
If a character hides the truth, readers may infer the character feels afraid or guilty.
If a character helps a stranger, that action can show generosity.

anchorCharts.name: Adages and Proverbs
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about adages and proverbs.
anchorCharts.body: An adage or proverb is a short saying that gives advice or teaches a lesson. Ask what the saying means in the story, not just what the words literally say.
ex: "Look before you leap" means think before you act.
"Many hands make light work" means a hard job is easier when people help.
"Practice makes perfect" means people improve by trying again and again.
"Actions speak louder than words" means what people do matters more than what they say.
"Slow and steady wins the race" means patience and effort can lead to success.

anchorCharts.name: Figurative Language
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about figurative language.
anchorCharts.body: Figurative language uses words in a creative way. Look for similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, idioms, and vivid descriptions.
ex: "The rain tapped on the roof like tiny fingers" is a simile.
"The proud mountain wore a crown of snow" is personification.
"The classroom was a busy beehive" is a metaphor.
"I waited a thousand years" is hyperbole.
"She spilled the beans" is an idiom that means she told a secret.

anchorCharts.name: Central Idea
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about central idea.
anchorCharts.body: The central idea is the most important point of a nonfiction text or section. It is bigger than one detail and is usually a full sentence.
ex: Topic: traditional tales. Central idea: Traditional tales often teach lessons through memorable characters.
Topic: tricksters. Central idea: Trickster stories show how cleverness can help or hurt others.
Topic: tall tales. Central idea: Tall tales use exaggeration to make heroes seem larger than life.
Topic: folktales. Central idea: Folktales can explain nature, culture, or important values.
Topic: proverbs. Central idea: Proverbs are short sayings that pass wisdom from one generation to another.

anchorCharts.name: Text and Graphic Features
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about text and graphic features.
anchorCharts.body: Text and graphic features include headings, captions, maps, diagrams, photos, charts, and sidebars. They help readers find or understand information.
ex: A caption under a picture can explain who a character is.
A sidebar can give background information about a culture or place.
A heading tells readers what a section is mostly about.
A map can show where a story or event happens.
A chart can organize facts so readers can compare them quickly.

anchorCharts.name: Literary Elements
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about literary elements.
anchorCharts.body: Literary elements are story parts such as setting, characters, plot, problem, solution, narrator, and point of view.
ex: The setting might be a dusty ranch, a village, or the sky above Earth.
The plot includes the problem, important events, and how the problem is solved.
The narrator is the voice that tells the story.
The problem is the challenge the character must face.
The solution explains how the problem is fixed or how the character responds.

anchorCharts.name: Theme
anchorCharts.imageAlt: A classroom anchor chart poster about theme.
anchorCharts.body: The theme is the lesson or message of a story. It is usually a full sentence about life, choices, or character.
ex: A story about a boastful hero who learns to listen may have the theme: Pride can make people miss good advice.
A story about neighbors sharing water may have the theme: Working together helps a community survive.
A story about a trickster who loses friends may have the theme: Cleverness should be used kindly.
A story about a child telling the truth may have the theme: Honesty builds trust.
A story about a small animal helping a giant may have the theme: Everyone has something valuable to offer.

passages.title: Why Traditional Tales Travel
passages.body:
Traditional tales are stories that people tell again and again. Long before many stories were written in books, families and neighbors shared them aloud. A tale might explain why the sun rises, why a river bends, or why a small animal can outsmart a larger one.

These stories often have unforgettable characters. A hero may be brave, a trickster may be clever, and a foolish character may learn a lesson the hard way. Because the characters are easy to remember, the lesson is easier to remember too.

Traditional tales also change as they travel. A storyteller in one country may add a mountain, while another storyteller near the sea may add a fishing boat. The details change, but the heart of the story often stays the same: choices have consequences, and wisdom matters.

[Sidebar: Traditional tales include folktales, legends, fables, tall tales, and myths.]

questions.q: What is the central idea of this passage?
choices: Traditional tales are always written in books.
Traditional tales travel, change details, and teach lessons through memorable characters.
All traditional tales are about fishing boats.
Only heroes appear in traditional tales.

questions.q: What does the sidebar help readers understand?
choices: The names of some kinds of traditional tales
The exact year the first tale was told
The author's opinion about mountains
The ending of every folktale

questions.q: According to the passage, why are characters important in traditional tales?
choices: They make the lesson easier to remember.
They always live near the sea.
They never make mistakes.
They keep every story exactly the same.

questions.q: Which detail supports the idea that tales change as they travel?
choices: A storyteller in one country may add a mountain.
Families shared stories aloud.
A hero may be brave.
Wisdom matters.

questions.q: Which saying best matches the passage?
choices: A story grows in the telling.
Never count your chickens before they hatch.
The early bird catches the worm.
A penny saved is a penny earned.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing traditional tales traveling from mountains to sea.

passages.title: Mara and the Storm Cloud
passages.body:
Mara was born during a thunderstorm so loud that the windows jumped in their frames. By age seven, she could whistle louder than a train and toss hay bales as if they were pillows. Everyone in Dusty Bend knew Mara was strong.

One summer, a black cloud rolled toward the town. It growled like a hungry bear, and the wind snapped at the rooftops. The townspeople ran to tie down wagons and shut barn doors, but the cloud kept coming.

Mara climbed the water tower and shouted, "You can roar all you want, but you cannot scare my town!" Then she began to hum the lullaby her grandmother sang every night. The sound floated upward, soft at first, then steady as a drumbeat. The cloud slowed. Its thunder faded. At last it opened into gentle rain that filled the dry wells.

Afterward, Mara did not brag. She helped patch fences and laughed when her little brother said, "That cloud just needed a song."

questions.q: Which detail shows that Mara is a tall-tale character?
choices: She can toss hay bales as if they were pillows.
She has a little brother.
She lives in a town.
She helps patch fences.

questions.q: What does "the cloud growled like a hungry bear" show?
choices: The cloud was quiet.
The cloud seemed powerful and threatening.
The cloud was really an animal.
The town had many bears.

questions.q: How does Mara solve the problem?
choices: She runs away from the town.
She uses a song to calm the storm cloud.
She throws the cloud into the river.
She hides in a barn.

questions.q: Which character trait best describes Mara at the end?
choices: greedy
humble
lazy
careless

questions.q: What is a theme of this story?
choices: Strength is always louder than thunder.
Courage and kindness can solve problems in surprising ways.
Never sing during a storm.
Small towns do not need help.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Mara singing to calm a storm cloud.

passages.title: The Clever Weaver
passages.body:
In a dry village beside a red cliff, the mayor owned the only deep well. He charged one silver coin for every bucket of water. "That is the rule," he said, though everyone knew the rule helped only him.

A weaver named Lina watched her neighbors grow thirsty. She carried an empty basket to the mayor and said, "I wish to buy the shadow of your well. Shadows cost nothing, yes?" The mayor laughed and agreed.

At noon, Lina placed her basket where the well's shadow fell. She invited the villagers to stand in the shade and rest. Soon the mayor shouted, "Move away! You are blocking my customers." Lina smiled. "But I bought the shadow. If you want it back, trade fairly. One bucket of water for every family each day."

The mayor frowned, but the villagers were listening. At last he agreed. Lina bowed and said, "A clever thread can mend a torn blanket."

questions.q: What problem does Lina notice?
choices: The mayor charges too much for water.
The village has too many baskets.
The cliff is too red.
No one knows how to weave.

questions.q: What does Lina's plan show about her character?
choices: She is clever and cares about others.
She is afraid of the mayor.
She wants all the water for herself.
She dislikes her neighbors.

questions.q: What does the saying "A clever thread can mend a torn blanket" mean in this story?
choices: A small clever idea can fix a big problem.
Blankets are more useful than wells.
Only weavers can solve problems.
Threads should be kept in baskets.

questions.q: What is the theme of this story?
choices: Rules should always help only rich people.
Cleverness can be used to make life fairer.
Water is not important.
Never stand in the shade.

questions.q: Which is the best summary?
choices: Lina buys a basket and walks near a cliff.
A mayor owns a well, so Lina cleverly buys its shadow and helps the village get fair water.
The mayor teaches Lina how to weave.
The villagers decide to leave their homes.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Lina the weaver beside the village well.

passages.title: Fox and Turtle Trade Tricks
passages.body:
Fox loved winning more than he loved being fair. One morning he challenged Turtle to a race around the pond. "Winner gets the basket of berries," Fox said. Turtle agreed, but she noticed Fox hiding a shortcut map under his tail.

When the race began, Fox dashed into the reeds. Turtle walked slowly to the bridge and called, "Fox, I found a basket even bigger than yours!" Fox stopped at once. He imagined berries piled higher than his ears. He ran back to see.

There was no bigger basket. There was only Turtle, still moving toward the finish line. Fox growled, "You tricked me!" Turtle blinked. "I thought you liked tricks. You brought a shortcut map."

Fox's ears drooped. He had lost because he trusted his own greed more than the path. Turtle shared the berries anyway, but she kept the map and used it to teach the younger animals where not to step.

questions.q: What is Fox's main character flaw?
choices: He is too sleepy.
He loves winning more than being fair.
He is afraid of ponds.
He shares too much.

questions.q: Why does Fox run back during the race?
choices: He wants to help Turtle.
He believes there is a bigger basket of berries.
He forgets where the pond is.
He wants to give up.

questions.q: What lesson does Fox learn?
choices: Greed and cheating can make a person lose.
Maps are never useful.
Turtles always run fast.
Berries should not be shared.

questions.q: Which proverb best fits this story?
choices: Honesty is the best policy.
All that glitters is not gold.
Practice makes perfect.
A stitch in time saves nine.

questions.q: How are Fox and Turtle different?
choices: Fox is unfair and greedy, while Turtle is patient and clever.
Fox is slow and Turtle is fast.
Fox is kind and Turtle is rude.
Fox shares berries and Turtle hides them.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Fox and Turtle racing around a pond.

passages.title: The Ten Lamps of the Mountain
passages.body:
Long ago, a mountain village used ten great lamps to guide travelers at night. Each lamp was carried by one guardian. The guardians took turns, so the path was bright but never too hot.

One evening, the youngest guardians grew bored. "Why should we walk alone?" they asked. "Let us all climb the ridge together." When all ten lamps burned at once, the mountain became a furnace. Pine needles curled. Streams shrank into silver threads. Travelers covered their eyes and stumbled.

The village elder lifted her walking stick and called the guardians down. "Light is a gift only when it is shared wisely," she said. Nine guardians lowered their lamps. One stayed on the ridge, glowing calmly until morning.

[Caption: In many legends, impossible events explain something in the natural world.]

questions.q: What natural idea does this legend-like story explain?
choices: Why one guiding light is enough at night
Why mountains are made of stone
Why people carry baskets
Why pine trees have needles

questions.q: What does "the mountain became a furnace" mean?
choices: The mountain was made of metal.
The mountain became extremely hot.
The mountain disappeared.
The guardians built a house.

questions.q: What does the caption help readers understand?
choices: A feature of legends
The exact size of each lamp
The name of every guardian
How to build a lamp

questions.q: Which sentence states a theme?
choices: The guardians used lamps.
The mountain village had a path.
Power should be used with wisdom.
Pine needles curled.

questions.q: Why do the youngest guardians cause trouble?
choices: They are bored and do not think about the results of their choice.
They want to help the village elder.
They cannot find their lamps.
They are afraid of travelers.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing guardians carrying lamps on a mountain path.

passages.title: The Drum That Would Not Boast
passages.body:
In a riverside village, every family owned a drum. Some drums were painted red, some were wrapped in bright cloth, and some were carved with shining birds. But the smallest drum, Kito, was plain brown wood.

Before the harvest dance, the painted drums bragged. "My sound will make everyone cheer," said Red Drum. "My feathers will sparkle in the firelight," said Bird Drum. Kito said nothing. He listened to the children practicing their steps and noticed that their feet often lost the beat.

On the night of the dance, a sudden rainstorm soaked the bright cloth and bent the paper feathers. The decorated drums sounded dull and uneven. Kito's plain wooden sides stayed strong. He gave a steady boom, boom, boom until the dancers found the rhythm again.

Afterward, Red Drum asked, "Why did you not tell us you were the strongest?" Kito answered, "Empty barrels make the most noise, but a useful drum keeps the beat."

questions.q: What character trait best describes Kito?
choices: boastful
humble and dependable
jealous
careless

questions.q: What problem happens on the night of the dance?
choices: The children forget the dance forever.
A rainstorm makes the decorated drums sound dull and uneven.
Kito refuses to play.
The village runs out of food.

questions.q: What does the proverb "Empty barrels make the most noise" mean in this story?
choices: The loudest bragging does not prove real value.
Barrels are better than drums.
Rain makes wood louder.
Only decorated things are useful.

questions.q: Which detail shows that Kito pays attention to others?
choices: He is made of plain brown wood.
He listens to the children and notices they lose the beat.
He stands beside Red Drum.
He talks after the dance.

questions.q: What is the theme of this story?
choices: Being useful matters more than showing off.
Rain ruins every celebration.
Small drums should stay quiet.
Painted drums are always weak.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Kito the plain drum helping children dance after rain.

passages.title: How Coyote Counted the Stars
passages.body:
Coyote was sure he was the cleverest creature under the wide night sky. One evening he told the rabbits, "I will count every star before sunrise. Then you must call me Master of the Sky."

He began proudly. "One, two, three..." The stars glittered like spilled salt across black cloth. Soon Coyote's eyes watered, but he kept counting. A sleepy owl said, "Rest first. The sky is larger than your pride." Coyote only laughed.

Near midnight, a cloud slid over the moon. Coyote lost his place. He stamped his paws and started again. By morning, he had counted the same bright star twelve times and missed hundreds more.

The rabbits did not laugh at him. They brought him cool water and said, "No one owns the sky." Coyote looked up at the fading stars and finally nodded. From then on, he counted what he could: tracks in the dust, berries in a bowl, and friends who gave kind advice.

questions.q: Which sentence contains a simile?
choices: Coyote was sure he was the cleverest creature.
The stars glittered like spilled salt across black cloth.
Coyote only laughed.
The rabbits did not laugh at him.

questions.q: What does Owl mean by "The sky is larger than your pride"?
choices: The sky is easy to carry.
Coyote's plan is too big, and he should be less proud.
Coyote owns the clouds.
Owl wants to count the stars first.

questions.q: What causes Coyote to lose his place while counting?
choices: A cloud slides over the moon.
The rabbits hide the stars.
Owl blows out the moon.
Sunrise comes immediately.

questions.q: How does Coyote change by the end of the story?
choices: He becomes even more boastful.
He learns to be more humble and to value advice.
He refuses to count anything again.
He becomes angry with the rabbits.

questions.q: What is a theme of this story?
choices: Pride can make people ignore wise advice.
The night sky has no stars.
Counting is never useful.
Friends should laugh at mistakes.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Coyote trying to count stars while rabbits and an owl watch.

passages.title: The Bridge of Borrowed Stones
passages.body:
Many villages tell stories about bridges because a bridge can stand for trust. In one mountain tale, two villages lived on opposite sides of a fast river. Each village had good stonecutters, but neither side had enough stone to build a bridge alone.

At first, the villages argued. "Our stones are stronger," said one side. "Our workers are faster," said the other. Then an old teacher drew a simple plan in the dirt.

[Diagram: Stones from both villages meet in the center of the river.]

The teacher explained that each village could build half the bridge, but the stones would need to lock together in the middle. If one side worked carelessly, the whole bridge would fall. Slowly, the villagers began to share tools, measure carefully, and listen to one another.

When the bridge was finished, children crossed it first, laughing over the roaring water. The old teacher smiled and said, "Many hands make light work, but trusting hands make strong work."

questions.q: What is the central idea of this passage?
choices: Bridge stories can show how trust and teamwork help people solve problems.
Mountain rivers are always quiet.
Only one village can build a strong bridge.
Children should never cross bridges.

questions.q: What does the diagram help readers understand?
choices: How the stones from both villages meet in the middle
What the old teacher ate for lunch
Why the river is fast
Which child crosses first

questions.q: Why must both villages work carefully?
choices: If one side works carelessly, the whole bridge could fall.
The teacher will leave the mountain.
The children want to swim instead.
The river will stop moving.

questions.q: What does "Many hands make light work" mean?
choices: A difficult job becomes easier when people help.
Hands can shine in the dark.
Work should only be done at night.
Bridges do not need stones.

questions.q: Which detail best supports the idea that the villages learn to cooperate?
choices: They begin to share tools, measure carefully, and listen to one another.
They live on opposite sides of a river.
The teacher draws in the dirt.
The children laugh over the water.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing two villages working together to build a stone bridge.

passages.title: Anansi and the Empty Jar
passages.body:
Anansi the spider wanted everyone to think he was generous. He carried a large clay jar to the market and called, "Free honey for all my friends!" The jar looked heavy, and the crowd cheered.

But Anansi had filled the jar with nothing but air. "Come back after sunset," he said. "The honey tastes sweeter then." He hoped the market would close before anyone asked for a spoonful.

A young girl named Ama watched the jar carefully. When Anansi set it down, it made no thump. When the wind blew, the jar rolled away like a dry leaf. Ama picked it up with one hand and asked, "Why is your heavy jar so light?"

Anansi's smile slipped. The crowd grew quiet. At last he admitted the truth. Ama said, "A gift that is only words fills no bowl." The next week, Anansi returned with a smaller jar. This time it held real honey, and he poured a little for everyone.

questions.q: What does Anansi want at the beginning of the story?
choices: He wants people to think he is generous.
He wants to buy a new jar.
He wants Ama to teach him to cook.
He wants the market to stay open all night.

questions.q: Which detail helps Ama discover the truth?
choices: The jar rolls away like a dry leaf.
The crowd cheers loudly.
The market has many friends.
The honey tastes sweeter at sunset.

questions.q: What does "A gift that is only words fills no bowl" mean?
choices: Kind promises are not enough without real action.
Bowls should never be filled with honey.
Words are heavier than jars.
Gifts should always be hidden.

questions.q: What is the solution to the story's problem?
choices: Anansi runs away from the market.
Ama hides the jar.
Anansi returns with real honey and shares it.
The crowd forgets about the honey.

questions.q: What is a theme of this story?
choices: Actions should match kind words.
Empty jars are always valuable.
Markets should close before sunset.
Spiders cannot carry clay jars.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Anansi holding an empty clay jar at a village market.

passages.title: The Moon Rabbit's Message
passages.body:
In one old tale, Rabbit lived on the moon and watched the world through a silver window. Each night, she saw people hurry through their work. They chopped wood, carried water, and counted coins, but many forgot to look at one another with kindness.

Rabbit wanted to send a message. She gathered moon dust, soft as flour, and shaped it into a glowing path across the sky. "Follow this light," she whispered, "and remember someone who needs you."

[Caption: Some traditional tales use animals to teach human lessons.]

Down on Earth, a boy named Jun saw the path while carrying firewood. He remembered his neighbor, who was too old to gather wood alone. Jun left half his bundle by her door. Soon the neighbor shared soup with a hungry traveler, and the traveler helped mend a broken gate.

Rabbit smiled from her silver window. Her path faded by morning, but the kindness kept traveling from house to house.

questions.q: What does Rabbit want people to remember?
choices: To look at one another with kindness
To count more coins
To hurry through every job
To live on the moon

questions.q: Which phrase is a simile?
choices: watched the world
moon dust, soft as flour
the kindness kept traveling
a broken gate

questions.q: What does the caption help readers understand?
choices: Why an animal character can teach a lesson
How to build a gate
The exact size of the moon
Why Jun carries coins

questions.q: How does Jun help his neighbor?
choices: He gives her half his bundle of firewood.
He teaches her to count coins.
He carries her to the moon.
He asks her to mend a gate.

questions.q: What is the best summary of the story?
choices: Rabbit makes a moon path that reminds Jun to help his neighbor, and that kindness spreads to others.
Jun carries firewood and forgets where he lives.
A traveler eats soup and breaks a gate.
Rabbit counts coins through a silver window.

passages.imageAlt: A poster showing Moon Rabbit sending a glowing path of kindness to a village.
